newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Siberian Chelyabenergo plays regional power game.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Siberian Chelyabenergo plays regional power game.

text.p: Hidden away in the wilds of the Siberian plains, one of Russia's biggest but little known power utilities, Chelyabenergo, is stalking foreign investment and grappling with the authorities in a fight for support.
Caught between cash-strapped industries struggling to regain lost output and the local government scraping for taxes, the utility has become an expert at political manoeuvring.
"As everyone is after money, I feel obliged to tell them I do not have any," one senior company official said. "We are prepared to overdramatise."
The company, which has seen its share price rise over a dozen times in a year to about $0.60 on the Russian Trading System, is open to investors. But it is cautious.
"We do not want to sell ourselves cheaply," he said.
NEW CLOUD OVER CITY SIGNALS STRONGER INDUSTRY

A pall hangs over swathes of Chelyabinsk, the first city with more than a million inhabitants east of the Ural mountains in Siberia. It is only 100 km (60 miles) from the Central Asian state of Kazakhstan.
Zinc, steel and other smelters that transformed the area from a Silk Road trading post to a closed Soviet town are powering up again.

Energy use, which has tumbled in the '90s under economic reform as factories cut or shut down production, has remained virtually unchanged this year for the first time since reform began, Chelyabenergo said.
Consumption up to the end of May was 12.15 billion kilowatt hours, against 12.28 billion in the same period a year ago.

The utility, which buys about half the region's power from other suppliers, saw its own plants' output jump 24.2 percent to 5.09 billion kilowatt hours. A plant it controls saw output rise to 1.93 billion kilowatt hours from 1.73 billion.
Chelyabenergo plans to sell energy outside the region by the turn of the century.

Chelyabinsk first deputy mayor Yevgeny Yeliseyev said industrial output rose three percent in 1996 on 1995, though it was still only about 60 percent of its level a decade ago. The first quarter also showed growth, he said, without giving details.
ENERGY USE INCREASING, BUT NOT CASH FLOW
But the sharp edge of regional recovery has forced Chelyabenergo into a tricky balancing act.
The rusting skeleton of a cooling tower with no funds for completion hangs over the company's Heating-Power Station Two.

Workers, who only received their March pay last month, are rushing to repair generators in time for a devastating continental winter but have no hope of improving generating efficiency with foreign parts -- there is no money.
"We get our grain from Canada and we may have to get our power from England," said Production Director Boris Mudrikh.
National electric company Unified Energy System (UES) has threatened to cut supplies to the region due to non-payments.

Chelyabenergo's deputy chief executive for economy, Nikolai Shchapin, said in a recent interview that cuts have not happened and that Chelyabenergo is a trusted partner of UES, but he says the situation in the region is not improving.

"Our plan for repairs is not being met and we cannot get enough coal," Shchapin said, adding that the company nurtures its customers and is loathe to cut them off. "We do not think we should be profitable while they are poor."

An internal company financial document said current receipts were 12 percent higher than current debts at the end of the first quarter, though a large percentage of receipts are in kind from metals producers and other customers.
Cash in hand was a miserly 0.1 percent of total debt.
"This low indicator of ability to pay shows decreasing payment discipline of customers and especially decreased collection of cash," the report said.

Debts owed to Chelyabenergo rose to 5.31 trillion roubles ($920 million) by mid-June from 4.13 trillion at the end of last year and are almost at the level of 1996 sales, which were 5.74 trillion. The company's debts have risen to 5.32 trillion roubles from 4.62 trillion, Shchapin said.

On paper the company's situation has improved, though. It estimated net profit to international accounting standards, based on Russian accounts figures, had risen to 365.25 billion roubles in the first quarter from 235.72 billion a year ago.
YOUNG REFORMERS COULD BE MAKING MISTAKE

A new threat with the potential to gut the company of its best payers comes from Moscow, where young reformers' plans to free the electricity market could mean the regional monopoly would have only a monopoly of poor clients, Shchapin said.
Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov, who is also a first deputy prime minister, has vowed to open up a national wholesale market so major factories can buy competitively priced energy.

"Why am I afraid of Nemtsov?" Shchapin asked. "The enterprises with no liquidity problems will go to the wholesale market. At worst, we will be left with the agricultural complex, households and the military. What can we do with them?"

Nemtsov also plans to reverse a system of cross-subsidies which forces industry, which in most countries pays the lowest energy costs due to its stable demand, to pay sharply higher prices than households, whose fluctuating usage in most countries demands higher prices.
Russia began a pilot programme from July 1 to reduce prices by up to 30 percent for industries which pay on time.
Chelyabenergo has its own plan of privileges for good payers and is cutting prices by three percent across the board.

But until the utilities' burden to support non-payers is eased, Shchapin, like many local power utility officials, views the free market warily. "The essense is that we have a tariff situation today that is not ready for that move."
($=5,763 roubles)
